doc.title: Paul Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 14, 1999

title: Liquid Sounds, counterpoint and staying home with family
summary: His early albums, including the Capitol Liquid Sounds group; he chose studio work to be home with his family.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Gosh, that’s very interesting. I’m looking at some of the recordings. You had a recording in ’53, was it “Fine, Sweet and Tasty?” Was this under your name?

Yeah. That’s one I just barely remember. It has come up constantly. I mean the first one that really was a semi-commercial success was “Liquid Sounds” which I did for Capitol, which was a little Bach group actually. It was six men, rhythm section, guitar, piano, bass, drums and a flute and clarinet. And I wrote the thing sometimes in four part harmony with electric guitar, piano, flute and clarinet, kind of like a sax section, and other times we have the counterpuntal stuff going on between the clarinet and guitar or flute and piano or whatever combination worked.
That counterpuntal type of writing seemed to ring a bell in the industry for a while.

Yeah, well that hadn’t been done at that time. I mean it was kind of a novel group. I mean it wasn’t a group I would take on the road because I deliberately wanted to be around my family. That’s one of the reasons I always wanted to be in the studio, so I could go home at night. I don’t want to be out in the middle of Iowa someplace in a club and then have to go back to the hotel. And at that time they allowed smoking in clubs so that really drove me up the wall.
Did you have children at this time?
Yeah. We have three. One we lost in 1988 in an accident, but we have three, two boys and a girl and five grandchildren.
So it was important to go home for you.
